newsitem.title: UK: Gunmen torch hijacked train in Northern Ireland.
newsitem.headline: Gunmen torch hijacked train in Northern Ireland.

text.p: Fresh Northern Ireland violence flared on Tuesday when masked gunmen hijacked a train and set it on fire.
Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam faced increasing anger from Catholics over a leaked official document which suggested she had ignored their objections to a weekend Protestant parade.

The train hijacking at Newry, 40 miles (70 km) south of Belfast, was the second such incident in an outbreak of nationalist violence that followed Sunday's parade by the Orange Order through a Catholic area of Portadown.
Police could not confirm reports that the gang told passengers they were members of the outlawed Irish Republican Army, which is fighting British rule of Northern Ireland.
The hijackers left behind them plastic bags thought to contain incendiary materials and the train caught fire. Passengers on the train at the time managed to escape.
The train was thought to be operated by Ireland's state CIE railway company which runs trains between Dublin and Belfast.

Mowlam held a new round of Northern Ireland peace talks overshadowed by Catholic ire over the leaked document, which concluded that allowing the parade along Portadown's Catholic Garvaghy Road was "the least worst outcome".
But it brought the worst unrest seen in Northern Ireland for years, blighting the year-old multi-party talks between pro-British Unionists and pro-Irish nationalists.

Participants say the negotiations are marking time, dogged by the alarming security situation in which two police have been shot and wounded, one hundred people hurt and the province gripped by nightly Catholic rioting and shooting.
Pro-British Loyalist groups emerged from the shadows of the conflict to stage an ominous show of force in which they said they would "defend" Protestant areas from Catholic attack.

Mowlam said that Catholic residents' groups opposed to weekend Protestant marches were not speaking to her because of the authorities' decision to allow Sunday's Orange Order parade over the objections of Catholic residents who felt it was intimidation.

She said she would continue to seek an agreement to avert further violence when the Orange Order marches along Belfast's Lower Ormeau Road on Saturday, at the climax of the annual marching season by pro-British Protestant organisations.
"Nationalists are very angry. Nationalists are thinking about whether to talk to me or not so my use may be limited after my failure in Garvaghy. I accept that," she said.

Mowlam disputed media reports based on the leaked Northern Ireland Office (NIO) document which purported to show that her advisers decided to permit the Orange Order march on June 20, 15 days before a decision was announced and greeted by riots.
The embattled British minister said the document was merely a summary of options drawn up by security advisers.
Catholic anger continued to burn. A policeman patrolling disturbances on Portadown's Garvaghy Road was shot and wounded as Catholics kept up a barrage of protest across the province.
Suspected IRA guerrillas or a sister group were believed responsible for his injuries and for a series of armed attacks on British troops and police during overnight Catholic riots.

Since Saturday night there have been 776 attacks on the security forces, 1,444 petrol bombings and 363 hijackings. A total of 60 police and 49 civilians have been injured and police and troops have fired 2,400 plastic bullets to quell riots.
To date Loyalists have taken no part in the violence. But Ulster Television showed footage of a show of force by six armed men who said their organisation would defend Protestant areas.
Some Protestants whose houses adjoin Catholic areas of Belfast said their homes had been targeted by Catholic youths in a nightly assault with petrol bombs and rocks.
Loyalists are officially observing a truce with the IRA they called in October 1994, but have been blamed by police for attacks against Catholic targets in the past six months.
